_version: The workspace version in Cargo.toml. scry never copies this onto the store row — it serves it beside the version actually published in its depot and flags the gap, so a tag ahead of a build shows up as a gap instead of vanishing. ci/scry_manifest.py --self-test keeps this equal to Cargo.toml, the same check release.yml already makes against a tag.

listing.blurb: Wake with nothing on a hostile island. Gather, craft, build, raid, lose it all, again. 100-player shards, one desktop binary, and a public server that is up right now.
listing.about: A survival game in the Rust tradition: an authoritative Rust-language server, a native Rust desktop client, WebTransport. The core is deterministic — same build, same seed, same input log, same world, hash for hash — so a round is one replayable file and a server can be checked instead of trusted. The skeleton is the product: netcode and determinism outrank every feature. Agents build it in public and agents play it; the same determinism makes the sim a training environment.

_listing: These fields are now THIS REPO's to write: whatever is here wins on the next pull, so editing them at scry's store desk is temporary and editing them here is permanent. Seeded byte-for-byte from the row as it stood 2026-08-11, so wiring this up changed no copy. Fields deliberately NOT claimed: state and play_url (the house decides when a title reads live), and capsule/hero/media (art is uploaded, not committed — a manifest is text and cannot ship bytes). band/hidden/placeholder/lane/note are the house's and a manifest may not write them at all.

updates.title: 0.8.0 — the distance stops fizzing, remote players stop teleporting, and the monuments are buildings
updates.body:
The far hillside stops fizzing. Every photographic texture in the game reached the GPU with exactly one mip level — no chain at all — so a 1024-pixel rock surface minified onto a slope two kilometres away folded in on itself, differently every frame the camera moved. That is the static you have been seeing on distant ground, and it was never an edge the anti-aliasing could find. There is a real chain now, built per image as it loads, and each map is filtered the way it deserves: colour is decoded before it is averaged, normals are renormalised, roughness is averaged plainly.

Remote players stop teleporting. Three separate starvations were stacked on one lane. A tick with no input from you used to walk your body at full stride, so stopping snapped you back — a starved tick now decays the last real frame to nothing over three ticks instead. Snapshots doubled to 30 Hz, which was the floor under every remote-motion defect at once. And the packet sent to recover from a dropped one used to throw away every remote body's motion history, so the recovery WAS the snap; it keeps them now. A respawn no longer slides your corpse through every wall between where you died and the beach.

Your own camera crosses the tick. The predictor steps on a fixed 30 Hz clock, so at 144 fps four frames in five were repeats of the last one, and eyes tracking the world read the repeats as smear. The view walks between the two predicted positions now. Aim is untouched — it still comes off the mouse at frame rate.

The item is actually in your hand. It was a sibling of the arms rather than a child of the hand, so the animation posed the fist and the tool stayed where the camera put it. The swing is a rotation of the whole assembly about a shoulder now, not a twist about the grip: travel over one stroke went from 26 cm to 2.24 m. The hatchet and the bow are held across the arm instead of along it, which is what a tool looks like in a hand. A landed blow throws debris — and a whiff throws nothing, because the server never announced one.

The world is built rather than boxed. The haven's shelter and the waystations' canopy were fourteen and nine grey boxes; they are modelled buildings. The island's 1,054 boulders and 746 ore nodes were drawn off two meshes between them — one rock, and one node wearing three different materials — and there are nine now, so stone, metal and sulfur finally tell themselves apart. Barrels, supply crates and cache boxes are their own objects, and the crate and the cache are deliberately tellable apart, because which one you opened decides what is in it. The road is a gravel surface rather than a line of pebbles standing on painted meadow.

This one breaks the wire — the packet layout went from 59 to 61, so a 0.7.0 client is refused at the door rather than quietly misread — and the world is wiped with it. 12 commits since 0.7.0.

updates.title: 0.7.0 — the shot lands where you saw it, the head is worth double, and the gun runs dry
updates.body:
A fight used to be decided by your ping. It is not any more. The shard now keeps the last eight ticks of every body's pose and resolves your swing and your bullet against where you actually saw the target, not where they had moved to by the time the packet arrived. The shard mints that rewind itself from what it watched you acknowledge — a client cannot ask for a bigger one — and it is capped at a quarter second, so a laggy shooter is compensated and a lying one is not.

Shots have anatomy. A head is worth double, a chest is worth what it always was, an arm or a leg is worth half, and the hit marker tells you which of the three you got — so aim is finally something you can learn by playing instead of guessing. A shot that clips a shin on its way into a chest is a chest hit; the rung is the most significant thing the line crossed.

Being shot points somewhere. A blow now tells the body it landed on which way to turn — sixteen bearing sectors, enough to face an attacker and not enough to snipe one blind. It comes from every route that can hurt you: a bullet, an arrow, a hatchet, a bear in the dark. Getting hurt also sounds like what hurt you, weighted by the blow, instead of one flat noise derived from a falling number — and a hit your armor eats whole is no longer silent.

The revolver has a cylinder. A firearm carries a magazine, it empties, and reloading costs you the same beat a swing costs — so missing has a price and a firefight has a rhythm. The rounds still in the cylinder when you die drop with the rest of you, so a killer loots a loaded gun rather than an empty one, and a magazine survives a save and a reconnect.

A torch is a torch. Held, it lights the ground in front of you; it burns a point of condition every six seconds and is a stick after five minutes; right-click puts it out. And other people can see it — a remote body now shows what is in its hands, so a bow, a hatchet and a lit torch are three different silhouettes. Light is visibility and visibility is a target, which was the whole idea and had never been true in both directions before.

Guns announce themselves down-range, an arrow you fired can be picked back up without a rifle claiming it was an arrow, and picking up your kit no longer drops the satchel out of your hand.

This one breaks the wire — the packet layout went from 52 to 59, so a 0.6.0 client is refused at the door rather than quietly misread — and the world is wiped with it, because the content moved. 76 commits since 0.6.0.

updates.title: 0.6.0 — armor goes on, arrows come back, and a base has a floor to build from
updates.body:
0.5.0 said armor was priced and the sim blunted a hit with it, but nothing could put a piece on. You can now. Wearing is a move rather than a button: drag a helmet onto your head the way you drag anything into a box. The slot lights when it will take the item and reddens when it will not, so a wrong-slot drag is answered before you let go. The wear panel says what a set is worth — each piece and a total — and the body is its own view now, so opening a box no longer undresses you.

An arrow you fired is an arrow you can pick up. It survives the shot about six times in seven, and one that hit somebody lies in them for ten seconds before it can be taken back — so an archer cannot re-collect the arrow they just shot you with mid-fight, and a bow still runs dry in a long one while losing almost nothing to a day of hunting. Arrows also stop passing through every floor on the island, which they had been doing.

Shots land on things. An arrow chips the wall it stops on, a bullet stops on the furnace it flies at instead of through it, and a hatchet marks the plank it hits.

Building has a floor to start from: a foundation pins the plate and everything latches to it, stairs walk the tread you can see rather than an invisible ramp beside it, a base has sides so the camera stays out of it, and a placement can decline the latch when you want it freehand. Twig stops wearing a photograph of a tree.

What you hold looks held. The item sits in the palm instead of the wrist, a rock is hand-sized, the revolver shows its profile, and the arm that is not holding anything is hidden. The island's ground is laid at its photographs' real size, a distant tree is a hull inside a triangle budget, and the renderer has a quality knob whose top rung is what shipped.

F7 writes a bug report a stranger can act on.

The platform is elo now and lives at elopros.com; the old host answers 410.

This one breaks the wire — the packet layout went from 48 to 52, so a 0.5.0 client is refused at the door rather than quietly misread — and the world is wiped with it, because the content moved. 75 commits since 0.5.0.

updates.title: 0.5.0 — the revolver fires, bodies fall, and a hit tells you where
updates.body:
The revolver was a dead end you could pay for: it dropped from barrels, it had a recipe, it sat on the research ladder behind gunpowder, and its rounds both dropped and crafted — and pulling the trigger did nothing. It fires now. Five shots to a kill, resolved on the server through the same path the bow already used, so what the shard says happened is what happened. There is no tracer yet.

A fight reads better. A killed body falls over instead of standing there. A hit body flinches, and a remote's swing is audible where it happened rather than at your ear. Arrows and swings leave marks on what they hit. A swing lands at the waist of anything shorter than you, which is what a stone hatchet against a boar should always have done. And the shard now tells the client how stale your aim was, in ticks, so a trade that felt wrong is something you can read instead of argue about.

You have a body: a face, hands you can see, and 53 clips behind them. First-person arms are the same mesh split by skin weight, not a camera trick. The streaming client stops paying for ground it already resolved, input is latched between sim ticks, and the frame is capped rather than spinning.

The wire is v48 and the save format moved with it, so this release wipes the public shard and an older client is refused at the door rather than quietly misread. Armor is priced and the sim blunts a hit with it, but nothing can put a piece on yet — that is the next thing.

updates.title: 0.4.0 — tools wear out, pieces line up, and the Windows build starts
updates.body:
Tools have condition. Every paying swing wears the thing in your hand, the wire carries the number so the client can show it, and a spent tool refuses the swing and says why instead of quietly doing nothing. A hatchet is a resource now, and one you logged off with comes back as worn as you left it.

Building lines up: pieces share a lattice, a solid deployable's top obeys the same step rule as every other surface you stand on, and structure damage reaches the client — so a wall coming apart is something you watch rather than infer.

The death screen offers the bag you actually have. The controls are the reference game's layout now, so eat is J. A panel that takes the pointer gives it back.

The island keeps getting its own paint: four ground surfaces with their own photographs and their own relief, and building pieces that wear one instead of a tier colour.

Discord can show what you are doing, if you turn it on. Presence carries the verb, the biome and your party size and locates nothing; sharing the shard's name and address is a second setting, off by default, and it is what makes Ask to Join appear.

Windows: the 0.3.0 Windows build could not start. It wanted a C++ runtime a stock Windows box does not ship, and died with 0xc000007b before a frame. The depot carries that runtime beside the exe now, and CI boots the staged build under wine before publishing it — the first check here that has ever confirmed a Windows build starts.

This one breaks the wire — 0.3.0 clients cannot join a 0.4.0 shard, so update before you connect — and the world is wiped with it, because the content moved. 34 commits since 0.3.0.

updates.title: 0.3.0 — raiding, the research board, and an island with its colour back
updates.body:
You wake with a rock and a torch now, and bare hands gather nothing — the rock is the bootstrap tool, and it is re-granted every time you come back. Eat and drink were dead buttons and are verbs again. The day/night cycle is 80 minutes, 70 of them light.

Raiding works end to end: a satchel planted on a real base breaches it on the live wire, a swing pays by stance and by which face of the wall you hit, and a hundred bots can raid at once without a cap giving way. Research is a board instead of a list — the scrap era's ladder, workbench tiers 2 and 3, and the blueprint-gated items that previously had no way in. Dying no longer deletes the blueprints you paid for.

The island reads properly now: four ground surfaces that were quietly sharing one texture, undergrowth that grows instead of reading as gravel, and a sun, a compass and a map that agree on which way east is. F12 takes a screenshot.

This one breaks the wire — 0.2.0 clients cannot join a 0.3.0 shard, so update before you connect. 124 commits since 0.2.0.
